content: Chorioamnionitis is a prevalent infection that impacts both the mother and the infant. In infants, complications associated with chorioamnionitis include early neonatal sepsis, pneumonia, and meningitis. For mothers, this condition can lead to significant morbidity, such as pelvic infections and septic shock. Clinical chorioamnionitis occurs in approximately 1% to 2% of term births and 5% to 10% of preterm births. Histologic chorioamnionitis is more common, being identified in nearly 20% of term births and 50% of preterm births. Women diagnosed with chorioamnionitis are at a twoto threefold increased risk of cesarean delivery and a threeto fourfold increased risk of complications such as endomyometritis, wound infections, pelvic abscesses, bacteremia, and postpartum hemorrhage. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of administering antibiotic regimens for intra-amniotic infection on maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality, as well as on infection-related complications. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving women diagnosed with intra-amniotic infection. These trials compared antibiotic treatment with placebo or no treatment, different antibiotic regimens, or the timing of antibiotic administration (intrapartum and/or postpartum). Diagnosis of intra-amniotic infection was based on standard clinical or laboratory criteria, and no restrictions were placed on gestational age. The review included 11 studies involving 1,296 women. The quality of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach and was found to be low to very low for most outcomes. The primary outcomes of interest were maternal and neonatal mortality, severe infections, and the duration of hospital stay for both mother and neonate. The antibiotics evaluated in the included trials were ampicillin, ampicillin/sulbactam, gentamicin, clindamycin, and cefotetan. During labor, a meta-analysis of two studies found no significant differences in rates of neonatal sepsis, treatment failure (endometritis), or postpartum hemorrhage when comparing two different dosages or regimens of gentamicin. No clear differences were observed in maternal or neonatal outcomes between the groups. The review did not identify any data comparing antibiotics with placebo or no treatment during labor. Postpartum, a meta-analysis of two studies comparing antibiotics with placebo after vaginal delivery showed no significant differences in rates of treatment failure or postpartum endometritis. Similarly, no significant differences were observed in rates of neonatal death or postpartum endometritis when antibiotics were compared with no treatment. Four trials comparing different antibiotic regimens (e.g., dual-agent versus triple-agent therapy) found no significant differences in most maternal or neonatal outcomes. However, one study involving 292 women reported a shorter duration of hospital stay for women who received short-duration antibiotics compared to those who received long-duration antibiotics (mean difference: -0.90 days). When comparing intrapartum versus postpartum antibiotic administration, one small study involving 45 women found that intrapartum antibiotic use was associated with a shorter maternal postpartum hospital stay (mean difference: -1.00 days) and a shorter neonatal hospital stay (mean difference: -1.90 days). Although no significant differences were observed in rates of maternal bacteremia or early neonatal sepsis, intrapartum antibiotic administration was associated with a significant reduction in neonatal pneumonia or sepsis (risk ratio: 0.06). The authors concluded that the evidence available for determining the most appropriate antibiotic regimen for intra-amniotic infection is limited. The quality of evidence was downgraded due to study design limitations, imprecision, and inconsistency of results. Only one outcome—duration of hospital stay—was supported by moderate-quality evidence when comparing short-duration versus long-duration postpartum antibiotic regimens. There is insufficient evidence to determine whether antibiotics should be continued during the postpartum period, which specific antibiotic regimen should be used, or the optimal duration of treatment. Additionally, no data were available on adverse effects of the interventions. One small RCT suggested that intrapartum antibiotic administration may be more effective than postpartum administration in reducing maternal and neonatal hospital stays.
